titulo: What Would YOUR Life Be Like as a Medieval Peasant?

cenas.texto: Imagine a job where your boss takes three days of your week, unpaid.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: And if your daughter wants to get married, you pay him a fee.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: And when you die, he comes to your house and takes your best animal.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: Welcome to England, around the year thirteen hundred.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: You are a peasant, and this is your life.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: Maybe you picture a muddy person, working every single day, and dead by thirty.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: Some of that is true. A surprising amount of it is myth.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: Did the lord really get to spend the wedding night with your bride?
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: Did peasants really work only a hundred and fifty days a year?
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: Today, we'll live one full year in an English village, from harvest to harvest.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: We'll plough, sow, reap, pay, and get fined.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: And at the end, we'll meet the disaster that hit your village hardest, and strangely helped your grandchildren.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Abertura (gancho: o que o senhor leva)

cenas.texto: First, you need a name. Let's call you Hugh.
And Hugh is not completely made up.
In 1279, King Edward the First sent officials around England to write down who held what.
In a village called Alwalton, they wrote down a man named Hugh Miller.
He was a villein, which means he held land from a lord, in return for work.
His holding was a virgate, which in Alwalton meant twenty-five acres.
That sounds like a nice big farm. It wasn't one piece.
Your land came as narrow strips, scattered across the village fields, mixed in with your neighbors' strips.
Hugh was in the middle of the pack. Alwalton had eighteen villeins with a full virgate, and five with half.
Below them, a crowd of cottagers, with a hut and a tiny plot.
England then had somewhere between four and a half and six million people. Historians still argue about it.
Most of them lived in the countryside, in villages like this one.
Above you sat the lord. In Alwalton, that was the abbot of Peterborough.
His estate was called a manor. And on a manor, the lord is landlord, boss, and judge, all at once.
Think of your village as a small company, where nobody asked you to sign the contract.
Our year begins on the twenty-ninth of September, Michaelmas.
The harvest is in. The lord's officials are adding up the year's accounts.
The villagers choose a reeve, one of your own neighbors, to boss the farm work.
Today, Hugh also owes a payment called tallage.
The amount is whatever the abbot decides.
Now you can start ploughing for winter wheat. In your own fields, right?
Not so fast. First, you work for the lord.
Hugh owes the abbot three days of work, every single week of the year.
He gets exactly three weeks off, at Christmas, Easter, and Whitsun.
In autumn it gets worse. He must send two men a day.
On some manors, the lord at least feeds you during that work.
So you plough your own strips on the other days, whenever the weather and the oxen agree.
Ploughing is slow. Walter of Henley's handbook for estate managers says a team does three and a half roods a day.
A rood is a quarter of an acre. So, less than one acre a day.
Walter loves oxen. He says horses cost more to keep.
Then comes the seed. Walter says you need at least two bushels of wheat for every acre.
And he warns: if your harvest is only three times the seed, you gain nothing, unless grain sells well.
So farming is a bet. You throw grain on the ground, and hope the weather pays you back.
A prayer book made for a rich knight, around thirteen thirty, shows ploughing with oxen, harrowing, and the lord's mill.
It's one of the best pictures we have of ordinary people from this time, drawn in the margins of a book for the elite.
By December, the fields are quiet. Time to go home.
Hugh's house is small, with one or two rooms.
In some regions, the animals live in the same building.
At Houndtor, on Dartmoor, archaeologists excavated a longhouse from the thirteenth century.
People and cattle came in through the same door.
The frame is wood. The walls are woven sticks plastered with mud. The roof is thatch.
In the middle of the floor, there's a fire. It almost never goes out.
There's no chimney. The smoke just drifts up and finds its way out through the roof.
Your house is also your smokehouse. Congratulations.
For a long time, historians thought houses like these fell apart within a generation.
But later medieval houses survive in their thousands, so many were sturdier than we imagined.
When the sun goes down, so does most of your day.
At Christmas, Hugh finally gets his week off from the abbot's work.
The church gives you more days off too. Sundays, and a long list of saints' days.
In winter, you thresh the grain, repair your tools, and mend your fences. Nothing glamorous.
Spring begins with a strange date: the twenty-fifth of March, Lady Day.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: In England, that was New Year's Day. The legal year started in March, not January.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: And it stayed that way until seventeen fifty-two.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Now you sow the spring crops: barley, oats, and peas.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Then comes Lent, forty days without meat.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: And here's a little secret of farming: spring is hungry.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Last year's grain is running out. This year's grain isn't ripe yet.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Cottagers feel it the hardest, with a tiny plot and no reserves.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: At the time, people believed a farthing a day, the price of a loaf, could keep a person alive.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: A farthing is a quarter of a penny.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Then Easter arrives, and Hugh's gift to the abbot is on the list.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Three hens, a rooster, and five eggs.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: Happy Easter, from your landlord.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Primavera: Lady Day e a fome

cenas.texto: So, what do you eat?
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Mostly grain. Around thirteen hundred, up to eighty percent of a harvest worker's calories came from it.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Grain shows up in three ways: bread, pottage, and ale.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Bread is dark and heavy, often made from barley or rye, not fine white wheat.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Pottage is a thick stew, boiled with grain, peas, and vegetables, and maybe a scrap of bacon.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Ale is brewed from barley, and it spoils fast. So somebody is always brewing.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Who? Usually women. Historian Judith Bennett found that women brewed and sold most of England's ale.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Meat is rare. A fattened pig can give you bacon for the winter.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: In the thirteenth century, harvest workers were given much bread, some cheese, and only small amounts of ale, fish, and meat.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: And those workers ate better than most peasants.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: So next time you complain about your sandwich, think of Hugh's lunch: bread, with a side of bread.
cenas.nome_capitulo: A mesa: pão, sopa e cerveja

cenas.texto: Then comes August, and the harvest.
This is the moment that decides your whole year.
Everybody helps. Wife, children, neighbors. All day, in the heat.
The grain is cut by hand, with a sickle, bent over, row after row.
And remember, the abbot gets two of your workers a day in autumn.
His grain gets cut first. Yours waits for the weather.
Then the sheaves are stacked, carried, threshed, and stored.
And now, the big myth. "Medieval peasants worked only a hundred and fifty days a year."
You've probably heard it. It spread from a popular book in the early nineteen-nineties, and it used the lowest numbers it could find.
Economist Gregory Clark looked again, and found that medieval farm workers worked at least about two hundred and fifty days a year.
Another study found that a farmer needed around three hundred days of work to feed a family before the Black Death.
So no. You do not have half the year off.
You get Sundays, a pile of saints' days, and three weeks free from the abbot.
If the weather was kind, you'll eat this winter. If not, keep watching until the end.
Every three or four weeks, the whole village has to show up for court.
It's called the manor court. Think of it as a neighborhood meeting, where you can be fined.
The fines are called amercements.
And everything is written down, on parchment rolls.
Some of these rolls survive. We can read what people actually got fined for.
In Morden, near London, in October thirteen ninety-nine, the court's ale-tasters reported brewers who broke the assize.
Their punishment was two pence per brew.
Others were fined for breaking the lord's hedges, or for trespassing on a neighbor's land.
In 1406, one man simply left the village. The court seized his empty land for the lord.
Judith Bennett found that this ale fine worked more like a licence. Most brewers were fined, whether they cheated or not.
So the "fine" was basically the price of a permit.
And who judged all this? Mostly tenants. People like you.
So when you complain about the lord's court, remember that your neighbors help run it.
And if you hate it all, you can run. Some villeins fled to towns.
A custom in many towns said that if a villein lived there for a year and a day, he became free.
But he had to stay hidden, and not be dragged back, for that whole year.
Let's add up Hugh's bills.
To the lord: three days of work a week, tallage, hens, and eggs.
If your daughter marries, you pay merchet.
Now, about that myth. Yes, merchet was about marriage. No, it wasn't what the movies say.
Historians have found no evidence that a "right of the first night" ever existed as a law in medieval Europe.
Merchet was a fine, a payment to the lord, perhaps for losing a worker.
Less movie, more tax form.
When you die, your family owes the lord a heriot.
That's usually your best animal.
Then the church takes the second best. That's called a mortuary.
Your family has just lost a person, and also two animals.
And all year, the church takes a tenth of what you grow. That's the tithe.
A tenth of your grain, paid in grain.
Do the math. Half of Hugh's working week goes to the abbot.
Plus a tenth of his harvest to the church.
And whatever is left has to feed a family, and pay for seed.
Hugh isn't doing this alone. Let's give him a wife. Her name is Alice.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Alice works the fields, cooks, raises the children, and probably brews the ale.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Everybody works, children too.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: A coroner's record mentions a ten-year-old boy hurt while chopping vegetables in a manor kitchen.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Historian Jeremy Goldberg estimated that one in ten rural people over fourteen worked as a servant.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Now, school. Can your son learn to read? Maybe. But not for free.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: A villein needed the lord's permission to send a child to school.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: In 1339, in Winslow, Richard Ponteys was fined three pence for sending his son Geoffrey to school without a licence.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Three pence for a school without paperwork. Bureaucracy is older than you think.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Some lords did give permission. At Norton, there were seventeen licences between 1300 and 1348.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: Why would a lord care? My guess: a schooled son is a worker who might leave.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Alice, as crianças e a escola

cenas.texto: So, how long do you live?
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: You've heard that people died at thirty.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: That's a statistic about birth, not about adults.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: Estimates for landholding families put life expectancy at birth around thirty-one.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: But so many children died young that they dragged the average down.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: Those who survived childhood often reached middle age, and beyond.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: Not that you'd be in good shape. No antibiotics, no vaccines, and not much help when you got sick.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: And what do you actually own?
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: Here's a real list. In the thirteen-forties, a coroner's roll in Derbyshire listed the goods of a man named John Fox.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: A house and ten acres. A mare and her colt. Some cattle, sheep, and a pig.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: A brass pot. A pan. Two chests. And some oats.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: That's a man with land.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: Historians warn that lists like this leave things out.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: But the picture is clear. Your net worth is a house, some land, and a pot.
cenas.nome_capitulo: Quanto você vive, e o que você tem

cenas.texto: So, how does Hugh's year end?
If he's lucky, with enough grain. If he's unlucky, like in 1315, it starts with rain.
In the spring of 1315, heavy rain began in England, and it kept falling.
The grain couldn't ripen. The hay couldn't dry. Food prices shot up.
The harvest failed in 1315, and again in 1316.
People ate the seed grain. And a smaller harvest came next year.
A few years later, a cattle plague killed more than half of England's cattle, by one estimate.
Your oxen were your tractors. So that hurts twice.
Then, in 1348, the Black Death arrives.
Historians estimate that a third to a half of the English died.
Villages like Alwalton would have lost many of their neighbors.
And then comes the part nobody expects. Suddenly, there were too few workers and plenty of land.
Lords needed workers. Workers wanted more pay. Wages rose.
In 1351, Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers: wages must stay at pre-plague levels.
It largely failed.
Over time, lords turned work into cash rent, and villeinage faded.
And in 1381, peasants marched on London, furious about a new poll tax.
Here's my take. In 1300, the lord was not your biggest boss. The weather was.
Too many people, too little land, and rain you couldn't argue with.
The weak spot of the Middle Ages wasn't kings. It was the thin margin between a harvest and a famine.
And it took a catastrophe to finally give people like Hugh some leverage.
That's a grim kind of progress.
Hugh never saw it. But his grandchildren might have.
So next time you complain about taxes, remember Hugh, who gave half his working week to the abbot.
If you enjoyed this year in the countryside, tell me in the comments: which life in history should we live next?
